card.hook: Here's a surprise: the best Hagia Sophia photo starts with a fountain. Put the water in front, that giant dome behind it, and the picture almost takes itself.
card.stand_here: Stand in Sultanahmet Meydanı, by the central fountain on the Hagia Sophia side of the square. Hagia Sophia lies about 400 m to the north-east, so face that way with the fountain in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the fountain, Hagia Sophia and maybe the Blue Mosque in together. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look at the building, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the dome and minarets, or to skip the crowds.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky and floodlit walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go just after dawn, when the square is quiet and the calm water can reflect the building. The square is busiest after about 9 am. After dark is the other sweet spot, when the building and fountain are lit up.
card.selfie_here: Try the Fountain of Sultan Ahmet III in Sultanahmet Park, on the east side of Hagia Sophia. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the dome and facade behind you, and come back after dark when the fountain lights up in colour. For a golden, lantern-framed shot, try the lantern-lined path beside Hürrem Sultan Hamam with the big dome behind you, though the whole building is harder to fit in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the fountain area in front of the building, so you're framed in front of the full facade and dome.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't allowed inside the building, and please don't photograph people who are praying. Hagia Sophia is a mosque with its own visiting rules, so check the official site before you go. Be wary of unofficial ticket and guide offers from street guides around the building.
card.challenge: Can you get the fountain, the dome and both a minaret and a straight horizon in one shot, with no stranger's elbow in the corner?
card.good_to_know: Emperor Justinian I had Hagia Sophia built between 532 and 537, and when it was finished it was the largest interior space in the world. It was a church until 1453, then a mosque, then a museum from 1935 to 2020, and it is a mosque again today. That long story shows in the outline: a huge central dome, stepped semi-domes and minarets added later.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Sultanahmet Meydanı, by the central fountain on the Hagia Sophia side of the square. Hagia Sophia lies about 400 m to the north-east, so face that way with the fountain in front of you.

card.hook: Look up the second you step inside: painted vaults, hanging lamps, and a passage that seems to go on forever. Everything is in your shot at once, which is the fun part and also the tricky part.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon, right in the middle of the bazaar. There's no single building to aim at, so pick a straight stretch of passage, face down it, and keep to the side so you don't block the crowd.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the vaulted roof and long passages. Switch to 1x for shopfronts and street scenes, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for lamps, ceramics and spices from a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of a display, then slide it a little darker so the lamps and glass don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go when it's less crowded if you can, so you get a clean view down a passage. Opening days and times can vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the Beyazıt Gate, across from Beyazıt Square and Istanbul University. Stand in front of the arch with the inscription and the sultan's seal (tughra) over your shoulder, use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit more in. The Mahmutpaşa Kapısı gate with its 1461 date is another option. Check both on arrival.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Beyazıt Square, across from the gate, while you stand in front of the arch so the whole gate fits in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing people. Shopkeepers may ask for permission or a purchase before you photograph their shop or work. Rooftop access is reportedly banned, so don't plan a rooftop shot.
card.challenge: Find a passage where the arches repeat evenly on both sides, line up the middle with the gridlines, and see if you can keep the walls perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: The Grand Bazaar (Kapalıçarşı means 'Covered Market') has 61 covered streets and over 4,000 shops. Its oldest part, the Old Bedesten, was begun in the winter of 1455/56, soon after the Ottoman conquest of the city. The rest of the market grew up around it over the following centuries.

card.hook: Count the minarets: six slim ones, standing guard around a dome that steps down in layers like a stone wedding cake. From above, you can see the whole thing at once.
card.stand_here: Go up to the rooftop terrace of Seven Hills Restaurant (Tevkifhane Sokak 8/A) and face the Blue Mosque, with Hagia Sophia right beside it. Prefer street level? Sultanahmet Arkeolojik Park gives you the fountain in front and the domes behind.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the mosque and Hagia Sophia side by side. Then try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the domes and minarets. Use 0.5x only for the full skyline, because it makes the mosque look smaller and further away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the main dome on a vertical third, and leave a little sky above the minarets.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun is behind you and lights up the front of the mosque. In the evening you'd be shooting towards the sun, so the mosque may look darker. Tap the mosque and slide the brightness down a touch if the sky looks washed out.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, hold your phone a little higher than usual and tilt it slightly so the domes show behind you. If your phone has 0.5x on the front camera, use it to fit more of the mosque over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The rooftop belongs to a restaurant, so you're expected to order something, and it may be closed in winter. Check the official site before you go. The mosque itself is closed to non-worshippers around the five daily prayers.
card.challenge: Can you fit all six minarets in one frame without them leaning over? Straight lines win bonus points.
card.good_to_know: The Blue Mosque is officially the Sultan Ahmed Mosque. It was built between 1609 and 1617 for Sultan Ahmed I, on the old Hippodrome site and facing Hagia Sophia. Thousands of mostly blue Iznik tiles inside gave it its nickname. It joined the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1985 and reopened in April 2023 after a long restoration.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go up to the rooftop terrace of Seven Hills Restaurant (Tevkifhane Sokak 8/A) and face the Blue Mosque, with Hagia Sophia right beside it. Prefer street level? Sultanahmet Arkeolojik Park gives you the fountain in front and the domes behind.

card.hook: Picture this: you've got Hagia Sophia at your back, and a huge stone gate straight ahead looking very pleased with itself. That's Bâb-ı Hümâyun, and it's the best way to open your Topkapı visit.
card.stand_here: Walk north-east toward the palace until you reach Bâb-ı Hümâyun, then stand directly in front of the main gate. Face the gate, with Hagia Sophia behind you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which keeps the gate's lines straight and the whole thing nicely symmetrical. If you're too close to fit it all in, tap 0.5x. For details high up on the gate, try zoom 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the middle of the archway on the centre line, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: There's no best time for the gate itself. If you go inside, guides recommend late afternoon light for the İftariye Kiosk terrace. The palace is a museum with closing days, so check the official site before you plan your visit.
card.selfie_here: Inside the Fourth Courtyard, stand on the terrace by the İftariye Kiosk's gilded canopy, with the Golden Horn opening up behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone slightly above eye level so the skyline sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks generally need prior permission from the museum. The gate viewpoint is free, but the courtyard terraces inside need a ticket, so check the official site first, including whether the terraces are open that day.
card.challenge: Get one tidy, centred gate shot, then wait a moment and take another with a few people walking through, so everyone can see how big it really is.
card.good_to_know: Mehmed the Conqueror ordered the palace built in 1459, a few years after the conquest of Constantinople. It was the main home and administrative centre of the Ottoman sultans from the 1460s until the mid-19th century. Topkapı means Cannon Gate, and it has been a museum since 1924.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk north-east toward the palace until you reach Bâb-ı Hümâyun, then stand directly in front of the main gate. Face the gate, with Hagia Sophia behind you.

card.hook: Taksim Square is one of Istanbul's busiest spots, yet the Republic Monument stands alone in the middle of all that space, like it's waiting for its close-up. Be quick, though, or your photo will fill up with strangers.
card.stand_here: Stand in Taksim Meydanı, on the south side of the Republic Monument, and face the monument. The Taksim Mosque is on the west side of the square, so it will sit off to one side or beyond the monument. Step a little left or right until the mosque sits neatly beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the monument with the wide square around it. Try zoom 2x to bring the mosque closer to the monument and cut out some of the crowd. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want the whole plaza, and expect the monument to look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the monument on one of the vertical lines, then tap the monument and drag the slider to make the picture a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go early in the day if you can, when there should be fewer people in the square. After rain, wet paving can give pretty reflections, so try holding your phone low.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Republic Monument in the middle of the square, with the open square and the monument behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and hold your phone a bit higher than your face. Lots of visitors take their picture right here, so you'll be in good company.
card.rules_and_safety: No general restrictions on photography in Taksim Square, though some private businesses may have their own policies. Don't stop in the middle of the street for a selfie; step to the side first. Access to the square can be restricted around certain dates, so check the official site or local news before you go.
card.challenge: Take a burst of shots and find the one frame with the monument, the mosque beside it, and not a single stranger walking through.
card.good_to_know: The sculptor Pietro Canonica made the Republic Monument, and it was inaugurated in 1928 to mark five years since the Republic of Turkey was founded in 1923. Taksim means 'division' or 'distribution', because the city's main water lines were once gathered here and sent on to other districts. The Taksim Mosque opened in 2021, and the Atatürk Cultural Centre, which faces the square, reopened in 2021 after renovation.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Taksim Meydanı, on the south side of the Republic Monument, and face the monument. card.hook: Picture a sloping street, café awnings flapping, and a big stone tower sitting at the top of it like the grand finale. That's the Galata Tower shot that actually looks like Istanbul.
card.stand_here: Stand on Büyük Hendek Caddesi, partway down the street, and face the tower at its upper end. Old facades, shopfronts and café awnings should sit on either side of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the tower and the street frame together. If the street is too narrow for the facades, or you're close to the tower's base, try 0.5x. Try 2x to bring the tower closer and keep strangers out of the corners.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, centre the tower between the two rows of buildings, and keep your phone level so the street edges look straight.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or just after sunrise, when the street is calmer and the light is softer. Crowds gather in the afternoon, so a clear view gets much harder.
card.selfie_here: Try the café-lined stretch of Büyük Hendek Street with the tower visible at the far end. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and check on screen that the tower is showing over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand well down Büyük Hendek Street, facing the tower, so the photo takes in the street, the cafés and the whole tower.
card.rules_and_safety: Some streets around the tower are steep and paved with uneven stones, so wear comfortable shoes. Stay alert to vehicles, deliveries and other people while you take photos. The street is open to everyone, but the tower is a museum with a ticket-control area, so check the official site if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the tower sits dead centre between the buildings and no stranger's head is poking into the frame. Patience counts as skill here.
card.good_to_know: Galata Tower is a round stone tower, 62.59 m tall, with 11 floors and a conical roof. The Genoese built it in the 14th century as the main tower of their fortifications at Galata. It has been a watchtower and a fire lookout, and since 2020 it has been a museum and exhibition venue.

card.hook: Most people rush to the big view and walk right past the arches. Here the arches are the trick: they frame the domes for you, like a picture frame you didn't have to buy.
card.stand_here: Walk into the outer courtyard of Süleymaniye Mosque and stop among the corner arches, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the domes and let the arches frame them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole courtyard and a few arches in. Switch to 1x for the cleanest, most symmetrical shot of the colonnade and domes. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out a single dome or the Golden Horn past the wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines so the columns and rooflines stay straight, then tap the stone of the colonnade and slide it a little darker to keep the sky blue.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon, when the stone takes on a warm glow. Skip prayer times.
card.selfie_here: Try the outer terrace behind the mosque, facing out over the Golden Horn with the mosque at your back. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a bit higher so the mosque fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of you with the mosque behind you, try the busy plaza at the western end of Galata Bridge and ask a passer-by to take it, then check the exact spot on the map.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship, so dress modestly and keep the flash off. Don't photograph worshippers, especially up close, and avoid taking photos during prayer times. Access to the courtyard and terrace can vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the one arch that frames a dome perfectly, with the columns dead straight, and take that shot before anyone walks into it.
card.good_to_know: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent commissioned the mosque and the imperial architect Mimar Sinan designed it. An inscription gives 1550 as the foundation date and 1557 as the inauguration date. It's the largest Ottoman-era mosque in the city and part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Historic Areas of Istanbul'. Behind the prayer hall is a walled cemetery with the separate mausoleums of Suleiman and his wife Hurrem Sultan.

card.hook: You walk down from a busy street and suddenly it's cool, dim and quiet, with 336 marble columns marching off into the dark. It feels like a film set, but it's a real 6th-century water store.
card.stand_here: Head for the Basilica Cistern, about 150 metres south-west of Hagia Sophia, and follow the phone icon on the map. Once you're inside, face down one long row of columns so it runs away from you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the rows of columns fading into the dark. Switch to 1x for a natural view along a single row, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the Medusa column base and the carved tops of the columns.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a lit part of a column, then slide it a little darker so the bright spots don't wash out.
card.best_time: The lights inside are artificial, so the hour matters less than the crowd. Go at the start or end of the day for fewer people in your shots, and expect slow-moving queues at the best corners.
card.selfie_here: Head to the two Medusa-head column bases in the far north-west corner and stand in front of them with the pillars behind you. Use the front camera, and if your phone has zoom 0.5x, use it to squeeze in more columns. Then take a short step to the Weeping Column, the one with teardrop-like markings, for a quick second backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the pavement across Yerebatan Caddesi from the cistern's main entrance, while you pose at the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: It's dim inside, so keep an eye on your phone and backpack. Photography and access rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the Medusa faces in the north-west corner and get a close-up where the face is upright and sharp. Bonus points if nobody's elbow sneaks into the frame.
card.good_to_know: The Basilica Cistern was built in the 6th century under the Byzantine emperor Justinian I. Its 336 marble columns, each about 9 metres high, stand in 12 rows of 28, and most were reused from older buildings. It opened as a museum in 1987 and was restored again between 2020 and 2022.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole arch and the facade, then switch to 1x for a more natural look. Use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for spice piles and sweets from a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the arch's sides straight, then tap the arch and drag the brightness slider down a touch so the bright outdoor areas don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, soon after the market opens, when the light is softest. Some guides prefer mid-morning, so arrive early and see how it looks on the day.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the main entrance archway with the bazaar behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the tiled arch fits over your shoulder, ideally in soft early light.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Yeni Camii Meydanı plaza by the New Mosque, far enough back to fit the whole brick arch, while you stand in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Many stalls have 'no photography' signs, so choose spots without them, and ask before photographing vendors up close. Selfie sticks are banned at many Istanbul tourist sites, so ask first. Stop walking before you shoot, because people get hurt looking at their screens.
card.challenge: Find the most colourful pile of spices or sweets you can, then frame it so the arch wraps around it like a picture frame.
card.good_to_know: The Spice Bazaar (Mısır Çarşısı) was built from 1660, after that year's Great Fire, as part of the New Mosque complex. Rent from its shops helped pay for the mosque's upkeep. Today it has 85 shops selling spices, Turkish delight, sweets, jewellery, souvenirs, and dried fruits and nuts.

card.hook: Picture a long, pale palace stretched along the water, with a ferry sliding past like it's on a schedule just for your photo. That's Dolmabahçe from the pier, and it's wonderfully calm.
card.stand_here: Walk out onto Kabataş İskelesi, on the waterfront promenade south of the palace, about 960 m away. Turn around and look back to the north-east, so the long sea-side facade stretches ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the facade and any passing ships. Try 0.5x if you want the whole waterfront in one frame, or 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for a tighter shot of a ferry in front of the palace.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then drag the brightness slider to darker, just a touch, so the pale walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Golden hour, when the white marble warms up. A few steps along the promenade give you new angles, so take a few shots as you stroll.
card.selfie_here: In the front garden, stand by the swan-shaped fountain at its centre with the palace facade behind you. Use the front camera and tilt it up a little so the palace fits over your shoulder. Another popular choice is in front of the Imperial Gate, with the gate as your backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the palace quay so the facade fills one side of the frame and a passing ferry or cargo ship fills the other, with you in the middle.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are either banned or 'not recommended' (narrow corridors), depending on the page, so stick to your arm. Photos inside have been restricted, so ask an attendant first and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a ferry to cross in front of the palace, then get the whole long roofline and the ferry in one straight, level shot.
card.good_to_know: Sultan Abdülmecid I ordered the palace, and it was built between 1843 and 1853. It's the largest palace in Turkey, with 285 rooms and 46 halls. Atatürk died here in 1938.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk out onto Kabataş İskelesi, on the waterfront promenade south of the palace, about 960 m away. Turn around and look back to the north-east, so the long sea-side facade stretches ahead of you.

card.hook: Here's a plot twist: from Sarayburnu the Maiden's Tower looks tiny, and that's the whole charm. You're not taking a portrait of a building, you're taking a picture of a little tower sitting in the middle of the Bosphorus.
card.stand_here: Stand in Sarayburnu (Seraglio Point), on the European side at the tip of the Historic Peninsula. Face north-east across the strait and the tower is out on the water in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the tower small in the whole strait. Go 0.5x for more sky and water (the tower gets very small), or try 2x-5x if your phone has them for a tighter shot. Take a few frames at different zooms, since the tower is small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the tower on a crossing point instead of the middle, keep the horizon on a gridline, then tap the tower and drag a little darker if the sky is very bright.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset is worth trying for warm light on the water. Check where the sun will be on the day before you set up.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Salacak promenade in Üsküdar, a shore walk close to the islet with the old city skyline across the water. Use the front camera at 0.5x and try to get the tower over your shoulder. Check the direction on the map first, since the tower is seen from that shore.
card.ask_someone: On the Üsküdar promenade just north of the ferry pier, ask a passer-by to stand looking south and slightly west, and stand where the tower ends up behind you.
card.challenge: Catch a passing boat or ferry next to the tower with the tower on a gridline crossing, and leave lots of water around it so it looks like it's floating.
card.good_to_know: The tower sits on a small islet about 200 m off the Üsküdar shore. A wooden tower was first built here in 1110, and the current stone version dates from 1763. It was restored from 2021 to 2023 and reopened to the public in May 2023. It's also called Leander's Tower, and one of the name stories involves an emperor's daughter and a snake.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Sarayburnu (Seraglio Point), on the European side at the tip of the Historic Peninsula. Face north-east across the strait and the tower is out on the water in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a pile of old brick, round domes and one skinny minaret, all squeezed together like they're sharing a secret. That's the Chora Church from outside, and it's a lot more photogenic than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, which sits on the church itself, so you can start shooting the moment you arrive. Then walk slowly around the building and look for angles where the domes and the minaret sit together.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for general views of the walls and domes. Drop to 0.5x where the streets are narrow and you can't step back far enough. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for brickwork, window arches and the minaret.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line up a vertical wall or the minaret with one of them, so the old brick stands up straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to old brick than midday sun. Going early on a weekday may also mean fewer people in your frames.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold your phone a little above eye level and tilt up so the domes and minaret sit over your shoulder. Take a couple of frames from different sides of the building to see which looks best.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working mosque, so check the official site before you go for current visiting rules, including whether photography is allowed. Flash isn't allowed inside, so rely on natural light.
card.challenge: Find the one spot where a dome and the minaret share the frame, then sneak in a little street or a few trees to show where you are.
card.good_to_know: Most of the building you see dates from the late 11th century, when it was rebuilt on a cross-in-square plan. The famous mosaics and wall paintings were paid for by the statesman Theodore Metochites, with the interior work done between about 1310 and 1317. The brick minaret was added around 1500, and the church became a mosque again in 2020, opening for worship in May 2024.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, which sits on the church itself, so you can start shooting the moment you arrive. Then walk slowly around the building and look for angles where the domes and the minaret sit together.

card.hook: You're standing on a chariot track, and most people walk right over it. The old Hippodrome was roughly 450 m long, and this open square is what's left of it.
card.stand_here: Head for Sultanahmet Square (Sultanahmet Meydanı) in Istanbul's old city: the obelisk is to the south-west of it, about 1 minute on foot. Stand near the Obelisk of Theodosius and face the Blue Mosque, with the obelisk base low in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the obelisk with the Blue Mosque behind it. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the carved figures on the base. Use 0.5x only if you want the whole square, and keep the obelisk away from the edges so it doesn't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the obelisk up with a vertical line, then tap the obelisk base and drag the brightness down a touch if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go early, before 9 AM, or in late afternoon for softer light and fewer people. The Blue Mosque makes a lovely backdrop at sunset. Spring and autumn are the busiest seasons, and summer midday can be hot and crowded.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the small pit around the Serpent Column, just south of the Obelisk of Theodosius, with the obelisk behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if you want more of the scene over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the central axis of the square at the northern end near the German Fountain, with you further along the axis, so you and all three monuments fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Be aware of pickpockets in the square, so keep your phone and bag close when you hand it over.
card.challenge: Find the emperor on the carved base, then get him in your shot with a minaret rising behind him.
card.good_to_know: The Hippodrome was the sporting and social centre of the Eastern Roman Empire, with stands for around 100,000 people. Theodosius brought the pink granite obelisk from Egypt in AD 390, and it was first raised at Karnak in about 1490 BC. The nearby Serpent Column was cast to mark a Greek victory over the Persians in the 5th century BC, and its serpent heads were destroyed in 1700.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Sultanahmet Square (Sultanahmet Meydanı) in Istanbul's old city: the obelisk is to the south-west of it, about 1 minute on foot. Stand near the Obelisk of Theodosius and face the Blue Mosque, with the obelisk base low in your frame.

card.hook: Picture a palace at your feet and a bridge that looks like it's floating over the water behind it. That's the view from the Asian shore, and it feels a bit like cheating.
card.stand_here: Stand at Beylerbeyi Sarayı (Beylerbeyi Palace) on the Asian shore, at the foot of the bridge. Face north-west and you'll see the bridge rise from the foot of its tower, with the palace in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the palace and the whole bridge into one frame. Then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and the deck.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the palace along the bottom, tap the bridge, then drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is lovely, and the bridge lights come on after dark. Want fewer people in your shot? Go earlier in the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to Ortaköy Square on the European waterfront, by Ortaköy Mosque, where the bridge rises right behind the mosque. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the bridge over your shoulder, and check on arrival which way to turn so it lands behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the square with the small Ortaköy Mosque in front of them, while you stand before the mosque so the bridge fills the background.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is for vehicles only, so don't stop or walk on it. Take your photos from the shore or from a Bosphorus boat.
card.challenge: Can you get the palace, the bridge and a perfectly level horizon in one shot, with a little sky left above the towers?
card.good_to_know: The bridge was finished on 30 October 1973 and is about 1,560 m long. Its two steel towers are 165 m tall, with a main span of 1,074 m between them. It was renamed in 2016, though plenty of people still call it the Bosphorus Bridge, and it has had colour-changing night lights since 2007.

card.hook: Picture a long, downhill street packed with people, and one little red tram sliding through the middle like it owns the place. That's İstiklal Avenue, and it's basically a ready-made photo.
card.stand_here: Head for Taksim Square, the upper (north) end of the avenue, and stand in Taksim Meydanı looking south-west down the pedestrian street with the Republic Monument in front of you. The middle of the avenue, around Galatasaray Square, is about 774 m away, roughly 10 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the monument, the width of the street and the buildings on both sides. Then go to 1x for the tram and the people. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to squeeze the long street together and pick out one façade or the tram.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the monument low in the frame, so the street leads the eye away from it.
card.best_time: Early in the day is usually quieter, so you get a clearer view of the street. Around dusk the shopfronts and signs light up and the whole avenue looks busy and warm.
card.selfie_here: Try Tünel Square at the lower end of the avenue, near the Greek Consulate area, or the spot right beside the Greek Consulate on the avenue itself. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the street sit over your shoulder, then check the shot and adjust on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo on the avenue just below Taksim Square, by the tram tracks, where the red tram comes out framed between shopfronts and overhead flags.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep an eye on your belongings, since pickpocketing can be a concern in busy parts of the avenue. Some passages, churches and galleries along the street have their own rules, so check the official site before going inside.
card.challenge: Wait for the red tram to roll into the gap behind the Republic Monument, then fire off a few shots and see if you can catch it with nobody walking through the middle.
card.good_to_know: The avenue is 1.4 kilometres long and runs from Taksim Square down to Tünel Square. It took the name İstiklal, meaning 'Independence', after the Republic was declared on 29 October 1923. The trams came back in 1990, when the street was pedestrianised and restored.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Taksim Square, the upper (north) end of the avenue, and stand in Taksim Meydanı looking south-west down the pedestrian street with the Republic Monument in front of you. The middle of the avenue, around Galatasaray Square, is about 774 m away, roughly 10 minutes on foot.

card.hook: Here's a view that does the work for you: the bridge, the water, then the domes and minarets stacked up in neat layers like a cake. Even a quick snap looks good.
card.stand_here: Stand on Karaköy Balık Pazarı, on the Karaköy waterfront on the northern shore of the Golden Horn. Face the bridge's Karaköy end, and you'll see it stretch across the water towards Eminönü, with the New Mosque and the Süleymaniye Mosque rising behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the bridge, the water and the mosque skyline into one shot. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the mosques in closer behind the bridge.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and set the bridge along the lower third, so the mosques and sky fill the space above, and keep the horizon level because the long deck shows every tilt.
card.best_time: The light changes with the seasons, so check where the sun will be before you set out. Its direction changes how the mosques and the bridge are lit, so tap the mosques and slide brighter or darker until the sky keeps its colour. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the busy plaza at the Karaköy (Galata) end of the bridge. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the skyline is over your shoulder. Check what ends up behind you before you commit, because this spot is better known for its view than for having the bridge directly behind a selfie.
card.rules_and_safety: Walking arrangements on the bridge can change, so check the signs on the day.
card.challenge: Walk onto the bridge and catch a fisherman at the railing with the Süleymaniye Mosque on the skyline behind. Bonus points if a boat sneaks into the frame (try a Live Photo).
card.good_to_know: The bridge you see today is the fifth on this site, finished in December 1994. It's named after Galata, the old name for Karaköy. The first was a wooden bridge from 1845, and in 1502–1503 Leonardo da Vinci drew up a single-span design, but the Sultan said no.

card.hook: Most people hurry straight past this corner of Eminönü Meydanı on their way to the bridge, and they miss the best view of the New Mosque's stack of domes. Don't be most people.
card.stand_here: Go to the raised platform at the northeast corner of Eminönü Meydanı, near the tram stop. The mosque is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot, so face that way and look out over the forecourt with the Galata Bridge in the same frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the forecourt, the mosque and the bridge all in one shot. Then try zoom 1x for a more natural look, and zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and minarets.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the domes, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out the stonework.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the square is calmer. Skip Friday around midday prayers, because the square fills up.
card.selfie_here: Use the open square in front of the mosque, with its domes and minarets behind you. Switch to the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck the mosque in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the raised platform at the northeast corner by the tram stop, while you stand out on the square toward the mosque, so they can fit the forecourt and the Galata Bridge in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working mosque, so keep photos quiet and discreet, and don't block entrances or prayer rows. Don't take close-ups of worshippers without asking, and avoid flash during prayer.
card.challenge: Get the domes, the forecourt and the bridge in a single frame, then zoom in and see how many of the mosque's 66 domes and semi-domes you can count.
card.good_to_know: Work on the mosque began in 1597 for Safiye Sultan, stalled after 1603, and restarted in 1660 under Turhan Sultan. It was finished in 1663 and opened in 1665. Its first name was the Valide Sultan Mosque, but 'New Mosque' stuck.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the raised platform at the northeast corner of Eminönü Meydanı, near the tram stop. The mosque is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot, so face that way and look out over the forecourt with the Galata Bridge in the same frame.

card.hook: A small, richly carved mosque, a lot of moving water and a huge bridge towering behind it: Ortaköy packs three postcard subjects into one frame, and you only have to point your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ortaköy İskelesi, the pier. Walk out toward the ferry ticket kiosks, then turn back to face the mosque, which lies to the east. You'll see it straight on with the bridge off to your right.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the mosque front-on. Drop to 0.5x to fit the mosque, water and bridge in one shot, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved stone and the two slim minarets.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the mosque on one side line and the bridge on the other, and keep the water's edge level.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely, when the sun drops behind the hills on the Asian side and softens the light on the mosque. People disagree on the best time, though: some swear by sunrise, others by sunset or dusk, when the bridge lights come on. If you're staying nearby, take a few shots at different times.
card.selfie_here: Head to the low stone wall in front of the waterfront railings, a couple of steps down from the main square. Sit or crouch, use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the mosque over your shoulder. The low angle keeps the shoreline clutter out of the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand in the main square just right of the mosque entrance, while you sit on the wall or nearby so the mosque stays behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working mosque, closed to visitors during Friday midday prayers. Photos are usually fine, but don't point your phone at worshippers during prayer, and the front steps may be restricted.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photo and catch a little boat gliding past with the mosque and bridge behind it.
card.good_to_know: Its formal name is Büyük Mecidiye Camii. Sultan Abdülmecid I commissioned it, and it was finished around 1854 or 1856. The architects were the Armenian father and son Garabet and Nikoğos Balyan, who also designed nearby Dolmabahçe Palace. After three years of restoration it reopened in 2014, and the bridge behind it is officially the 15 July Martyrs Bridge.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ortaköy İskelesi, the pier. Walk out toward the ferry ticket kiosks, then turn back to face the mosque, which lies to the east. You'll see it straight on with the bridge off to your right.

card.hook: Broad brick walls, a roof that steps up and down towards the dome, and trees to soften it all: Hagia Irene is the calm, sturdy one in Topkapı's outer courtyard.
card.stand_here: Head for the First Courtyard of Topkapı Palace and step back to the west approach, near the phone icon at the centre of the building's outline. Face the long side of Hagia Irene so the whole wall and dome fit in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from the west approach so the whole brick side and the dome fit. Then try 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out the different roof heights without walking closer. Use 0.5x only if you're tight against the wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up a vertical wall edge with a grid line so the brickwork stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: There's no fixed best time. Soft light early or late in the day usually flatters brick, and a quieter courtyard makes it easier to get the whole building without people in the way.
card.selfie_here: Try the open ground in front of the church's outer walls in the exterior courtyard, inside the first courtyard of Topkapı Palace. Enter through the Imperial Gate and turn to the building on your right. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the church fill the space over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside Hagia Irene is generally allowed for personal use, but check the staff signs, especially for flash. Flash or photography can be restricted during events, so follow posted instructions.
card.challenge: Count how many different roof levels you can fit in one shot, then see if a friend gets more.
card.good_to_know: Hagia Irene means "Holy Peace" and is the oldest known church structure in Istanbul. After 1453 it sat inside the palace walls and was used as an arsenal, which is why it never became a mosque. It was burned in the Nika revolt of 532, rebuilt in 548 under Justinian I, and is now a museum and concert hall. Museum entry is separate, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the First Courtyard of Topkapı Palace and step back to the west approach, near the phone icon at the centre of the building's outline. Face the long side of Hagia Irene so the whole wall and dome fit in.

card.hook: You're squeezed between market stalls in Tahtakale, then you glance up and a whole mosque is sitting on top of the shops. Rüstem Pasha is small and easy to walk past, but the tiles under its porch are worth the neck-craning.
card.stand_here: Stand on Hasırcılar Caddesi, on the west side, and face north-east. The raised, tiled porch rises above you, with the main entrance on the north side.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole façade. If the street is too tight for the porch, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tile panels and porch columns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the terrace level, then tap the tiled porch and slide the brightness a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out the colours.
card.best_time: Go early in the day. The lanes are quieter, so it's easier to step back and get the whole façade in.
card.selfie_here: Climb the stone stairs from Hasırcılar Caddesi to the terrace at the top, then use the front camera with the colonnaded porch behind you. For a street shot, try the small street running north off Hasırcılar Caddesi, facing the Golden Horn with the mosque behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small street running north off Hasırcılar Caddesi, about where the stairs begin, while you pose with the mosque and its stairs above you.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside, take your shoes off, keep out of the prayer area, skip the flash and dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered, and women should cover their heads). The stairs have many steps and no ramp or lift, and opening times can change, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Fill your frame with nothing but tiles, then take one step back at a time until the shops sneak in at the bottom.
card.good_to_know: The great architect Mimar Sinan designed this mosque for Rüstem Pasha, a Grand Vizier under Suleiman I, and it was finished around 1563. Inside there are roughly 2,300 İznik tiles in about 80 patterns. It was once used for film storage and reopened for worship in 2021 after a long restoration.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Hasırcılar Caddesi, on the west side, and face north-east. The raised, tiled porch rises above you, with the main entrance on the north side.
